subject: OT
topic: Who is a Prophet?
front: What are the three Hebrew words used to designate a prophet?
back: Nāvi, rõ'eh and hõzeh.
excerpt:
In the Old Testament, three Hebrew words are normally used to designate the Prophets. 
These are Nāvi, rõ'eh and hõzeh.

subject: OT
topic: Who is a Prophet?
front: What is a Nāvi?
back: One who speaks forth for God. Aaron was Moses' Nāvi: Moses stood in relation to Pharaoh as God, and Aaron spoke to Pharaoh on behalf of Moses.
excerpt:
The man who can be designated a "Ntivi", then is one who speaks 
forth for God.

subject: OT
topic: Who is a Prophet?
front: Define a prophet in the Old Testament.
back: A person who receives a message from God and utters the actual words that God has given him, without any modification or interpretation on his part (Deut. 18:18).
excerpt:
A prophet in the Old Testament then is a person who receives a message from God 
and utters the actual words that God has given to him, without any modification or 
interpretation on his part.

subject: OT
topic: The Establishment of the Prophetic Institution
front: Why was the Law alone not adequate for Israel's life in Canaan?
back: Not through any inherent weakness in the Law, but because it did not speak in detail on every possible situation that would arise in Israel's life. A specific revelation was needed, and God gave it through the prophets.
excerpt:
This inadequacy was not due to any inherent weakness in the 
Law itself, but simply to the fact that the Law did not speak in detail on every possible 
situation that would arise in Israel's life.

subject: OT
topic: The Establishment of the Prophetic Institution
front: Who founded the bands (hevel) of prophets, and when did such bands reappear?
back: Samuel is believed to have founded them. They seem to have disbanded after his death and are not heard of again until the times of Elijah and Elisha, when they reappeared in the Northern Kingdom as the "sons of the prophets".
excerpt:
It is believed that Samuel was the founder of such groups. Following the death of Samuel, 
these prophetical bodies seem to have disbanded.

subject: OT
topic: Forms of Prophets and Prophetic Groups in Israel
front: What are the three main forms of Old Testament prophecy?
back: The Company of Prophets, the Royal Cults or Court Prophets, and Individual Prophets.
excerpt:
broadly speaking the Old Testament prophecy falls into three main forms: The Company of 
Prophets, the Royal Cults or Court Prophets and Individual Prophets.

subject: OT
topic: Facts about Prophecy in Israel
front: What does the word "prophecy" properly mean in the Old Testament?
back: To speak the word of God — not, as is popularly supposed, to predict the future.
excerpt: In the Old Testament the word means To Speak the Word of God.

subject: OT
topic: Facts about Prophecy in Israel
front: What is prophetic action, or prophetic symbolism?
back: An acted sign which is itself creative of what it depicts — for example, Ezekiel building a city on sand and making a toy soldier (Ezekiel 4). The prophetic actions were believed to contain power to shape the future.
excerpt:
The prophetic action is itself creative of what it depicts. For example, 
Ezekiel builds a city on sand with mud and makes a toy soldier (Ezekiel 4) etc.

subject: OT
topic: Facts about Prophecy in Israel
front: What are the three tests for distinguishing a true from a false prophet?
back: The theological test (Deut. 13), the practical test (Deut. 18:20ff) and the moral test (Jer. 23:9ff).
excerpt:
In the Old Testament, there were three tests which the people could use to discern between 
true and false prophets.

subject: OT
topic: Facts about Prophecy in Israel
front: Why is the practical test (Deut. 18:20ff) called a negative test?
back: Because it says only that what is not fulfilled is not from the Lord. It does not say that fulfilment proves the Lord has spoken, since a false prophet might offer fulfilment as evidence for his own word.
excerpt: It must be noted that, this is a negative test. It does not say that fulfillment is proof that the Lord has spoken

subject: OT
topic: Facts about Prophecy in Israel
front: How many false prophets stood against Micaiah in 1 Kings 22?
back: Four hundred. Micaiah son of Imlah was the only true prophet, and his word proved true when Ahab died in battle.
excerpt:
For example, in 1 
Kings 22, there were 400 false prophets and Micaiah was the only true prophet.

subject: OT
topic: INTRODUCTION
front: How are the books of the Hebrew Old Testament arranged?
back: In three parts — the Law, the Prophets and the Writings.
excerpt:
The books of the Hebrew Old Testament are arranged in three parts - the Law, the Prophets 
and the Writings.

subject: OT
topic: The Books of the Old Testament that Constitute the Prophets
front: Which books make up the Former Prophets?
back: Joshua, Judges, I & II Samuel and I & II Kings.
excerpt: The Former Prophets: The books are: Joshua, Judges, I & II Samuel and I & II Kings

subject: OT
topic: The Books of the Old Testament that Constitute the Prophets
front: What period do the Former Prophets cover?
back: From Israel's entrance into the Promised Land until the destruction of the theocracy under Nebuchadnezzar.
excerpt:
The 
former prophets cover the period from Israel's entrance into the Promised Land until the 
destruction of the theocracy under Nebuchadnezzar.

subject: OT
topic: The Books of the Old Testament that Constitute the Prophets
front: Who are the Major and the Minor Prophets?
back: Major Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel. Minor Prophets: the Twelve, from Hosea to Malachi. Together they form the Latter or Writing Prophets.
excerpt: Major Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel

subject: OT
topic: Deuteronomy and the Former Prophets
front: What is the "Deuteronomic" view of history?
back: The presentation of Israel's history along the lines of Moses' teaching in Deuteronomy: obedience brings blessing seen in national strength and victory, while disobedience brings punishment seen in weakness and invasion.
excerpt:
The style or interpretation of history is a reflection of what Moses said 
in the Book of Deuteronomy, hence what is referred to as "Deuteronomic" view of history.

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
front: Why was Joshua defeated at Ai?
back: Because Achan coveted some of the spoils from Jericho and kept them for himself instead of letting all be offered to God. He and his family were totally destroyed — a grim illustration that disobedience brings disaster.
excerpt:
The reason for this defeat was because Achan coveted some of the spoils from Jericho 
and kept them for himself instead of letting it all be offered to God.

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
front: What period does the book of Judges cover?
back: The period between Joshua's death and the rise of Samuel, roughly 1220 to 1050 B.C.
excerpt:
Judges covers the period in Israel's history between Joshua's death and the rise of Samuel - 
roughly 1220 to 1050 B.C.

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
front: What explanation do Judges 17:6 and 21:25 give for the moral decline of the period?
back: "There was no King in Israel and every man did what was right in his own eyes."
excerpt:
the explanation given for this state of affairs is that, "There was no 
King in Israel and every man did what was right in his own eyes".

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
front: Why are the books of Samuel named after him?
back: Not because he wrote them, but because he is the dominating figure. He is seen as the king maker, who anointed both Saul and David as kings.
excerpt:
The name Samuel is given to the books not because he is the writer, but because he is 
the dominating figure. He is seen in the book as the King maker - he anointed both Saul and 
David as Kings.

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
front: What period do the books of Kings cover?
back: Four centuries — from the close of David's reign (930 B.C.), through Solomon and the divided kingdom, to the fall of Samaria in 722 B.C. and the destruction of Jerusalem in 587 B.C., ending with the release of Jehoiachin after 561 B.C.
excerpt:
to the fall of Samaria in 722 BC and the 
destruction of Jerusalem in 587 BC, and ends with the release of Jehoiachin

subject: OT
topic: Background - The Conflict between Yahwism and Baalism during the Settlement in the land of Canaan
front: When did Elijah and Elisha prophesy?
back: Elijah, who came from Tishbe in Gilead, prophesied during the reign of Ahab (c. 873-851 B.C.); Elisha's ministry ran from the time of Ahab through to the reign of Jehoahaz (c. 815-800 B.C.).
excerpt:
the Prophet Elijah, who came 
from Tishbe in Gilead prophesied during the reign of Ahab (c. 873 -851 B.C.), while Elisha's 
ministry was from the period of Ahab through to the reign of Jehoahaz

subject: OT
topic: Background - The Conflict between Yahwism and Baalism during the Settlement in the land of Canaan
front: Describe Yahwism.
back: The Israelite religion, holding a position of monolatry or henotheism — worship given exclusively to Yahweh. It abhors visual representation, lays no stress on sanctuaries or sacred places, and lays strong emphasis on morality and the keeping of the Sinai commandments.
excerpt:
Yahwism, the Israelite religion, has a theological position of monolatry or henotheism, (i.e. 
worship was to be given exclusively to Yahweh). It abhors visual representation of any kind.

subject: OT
topic: Background - The Conflict between Yahwism and Baalism during the Settlement in the land of Canaan
front: Describe Baalism.
back: A religion tied to the land, of times and seasons; purely agricultural, laying great emphasis on local shrines, sanctuaries and high places; polytheistic, connected with the fertility of the land, and laying no stress at all on morality.
excerpt:
Baalism, by contrast, was a religion tied to the land, a religion of times and seasons. It was 
purely an agricultural religion that laid great emphasis on local shrines, sanctuaries, and high places.

subject: OT
topic: Background - The Conflict between Yahwism and Baalism during the Settlement in the land of Canaan
front: Who were the Rechabites?
back: An example of those who would not compromise at all in their strict obedience to Yahwism (Jer. 35:1-17), over against the general Israelite pattern of compromise with Baalism.
excerpt:
The Rechabites (see Jer. 35:1-17) were an example of 
those who would not compromise at all on their strict obedience to Yahwism.

subject: OT
topic: The Traditions of Elijah and Elisha
front: What is the difference between the traditions of Elijah and those of Elisha?
back: Elijah's traditions turn on the clash between Yahwism and Baalism — the drought, the Mount Carmel contest, Naboth, and the oracles against Ahaziah. Elisha's do not show that tension, but the performance of signs and wonders at personal and national levels.
excerpt:
Elisha's traditions, however, do not show the same tension between Yahwism and Baalisrn, 
but that of the performance of Signs and Wonders both at personal and national levels

subject: OT
topic: The Prophet Amos
front: What does the name Amos mean?
back: "Burden-bearer". He is the only man in the Old Testament with this name, and it should not be confused with Amoz, the father of Isaiah.
excerpt: The Name Amos: Amos means "burden-bearer." He is the only man in the Old Testament with this name.

subject: OT
topic: The Prophet Amos
front: What is Amos's place among the prophets?
back: He is regarded as the first of the classical prophets and ranks as the greatest of the Minor Prophets.
excerpt:
He is regarded as the first of the classical 
prophets and ranks as the greatest of the Minor Prophets.

subject: OT
topic: The Prophet Amos
front: Where was Tekoa?
back: A small mountain-top town in Judah, about twelve miles from Jerusalem and about six miles south east of Bethlehem, believed to be the centre of a large sheep-farming district.
excerpt:
Tekoa was about twelve (12) miles from Jerusalem, the capital of the Southern 
Kingdom and about six (6) miles south east of Bethlehem.

subject: OT
topic: The Prophet Amos
front: What does the term nõqĕd, used of Amos in Amos 1:1, mean?
back: The keeper of a particular kind of desert sheep, highly priced for the excellence of their wool. Properly interpreted it refers to a sheep owner who had other shepherds under him, which suggests Amos was a substantial and respected man.
excerpt:
The term nõqĕd 
was used to describe the keeper of a particular kind of desert sheep that were highly priced 
on account of the excellence of their wool.

subject: OT
topic: The Historical Background to Amos' Ministry
front: During whose reign did Amos prophesy?
back: Jeroboam II, who ruled Israel from 786 to 746 B.C. — the period when the fortunes of the Northern Kingdom stood at their highest point of prosperity and peace.
excerpt: Amos delivered his message during the reign of Jeroboam II, who ruled Israel from 786 to 746 BC.

subject: OT
topic: Socio-Economic Situation
front: What were the economic policies of Jeroboam II?
back: The imposition of tolls upon all caravans passing through Israel, increased opportunities for international trade, and the development of Samaria into a strong commercial centre.
excerpt:
The imposition of tolls upon all caravans passing through Israel. This brought a lot of 
revenue to the treasury.

subject: OT
topic: Socio-Economic Situation
front: What was the one important feature of the socio-economic situation in Amos's day?
back: The rich became richer while the poor became poorer. Amos repeatedly attacked this division, especially the luxury of the rich set against the misery of the poor.
excerpt:
One important feature of the period was that the rich became richer while the poor became 
poorer.

subject: OT
topic: Religious Situation
front: What are "bacchanalian orgies"?
back: Noisy drunkenness, dancing and other merrymaking associated with the worship of the god Bacchus, the god of wine; they were part of the fertility cults of the surrounding nations and had invaded Israel's worship.
excerpt:
bacchanalian orgies (noisy, drunkenness, dancing and other merrymaking associated with the worship of the god 
Bacchus (the god of wine)

subject: OT
topic: The Ministry of Amos
front: What did Amos mean by "I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son"?
back: That he was not a professional prophet, nor a member of the schools of prophets. It made no difference, because it is God's calling that makes the prophet.
excerpt: He was not a professional prophet ("I was no prophet"), nor a member of the schools of prophets ("neither was I a prophet's son").

subject: OT
topic: The Ministry of Amos
front: What does "Bethel" mean, and what had it become by Amos's day?
back: "House of God" — Jacob gave the name to the place formerly known as Luz. After the division of the kingdom in 931 B.C. it became one of the two major religious sites of the North, where the golden calf was worshipped, so that the house of God became the house of iniquity.
excerpt:
which motivated him to give the 
name "Bethel" (meaning "House of God") to the place, which was formerly known as Luz (Gen 28: 19).

subject: OT
topic: The Ministry of Amos
front: Where is the essence of the teaching of Amos found?
back: In Amos 5:24. His message is dominated by the idea of God's righteousness.
excerpt: The essence of the teaching of Amos is found in Amos 5:24.

subject: OT
topic: The Ministry of Amos
front: What does "righteousness" mean in the Old Testament?
back: It belongs to the vocabulary of salvation and is a covenant word. Of God it means his faithfulness in keeping his covenant; of people, their faithfulness in keeping it. It is not a legal but a moral and spiritual concept.
excerpt: Righteousness is a covenant word, and the righteousness of God refers to God's faithfulness in keeping His covenant.

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
front: What is the significance of the oracles against the nations?
back: They indicate Yahweh's sovereignty beyond his covenant people. God is portrayed as the King of his world who judges sin and unrighteousness wherever it occurs; he is ruler of all nations and all people stand under his authority.
excerpt:
The significance of the prophecy against the nations is to indicate the concept of Yahweh's 
sovereignty beyond His covenant people.

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
front: Which nations and capitals are named in the eight oracles of Amos?
back: Syria (Damascus), Philistia (Gaza), Phoenicia (Tyre), Edom (Teman and Bozrah), Ammon (Rabbah), Moab (Kirioth), Judah (Jerusalem) and Israel (Samaria).
excerpt: Syria - Capital City, DAMASCUS (1:3-5).

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
front: What are the five visions of doom in Amos?
back: The locust plague (7:1-3), the vision of fire (7:4-6), the plumb line (7:7-16), the basket of summer fruit (8:1-14) and the Lord at the altar (9:1-10).
excerpt:
The Locust Plagues 7: 1-3: God revealed to Amos in a vision that the crops were to be 
destroyed by an invasion of locusts.

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
front: What did the basket of summer fruit signify?
back: Israel, which was now ripe for judgment.
excerpt:
He then explained to Amos that it symbolized Israel which was now 
ripe for judgment.

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
front: What five restorations does Amos promise at the close of his book?
back: The restoration of the Davidic dynasty (9:11a), of unity in the nation (9:11b-12), of agriculture (9:13), of the people (9:14a) and of liberty (9:14b).
excerpt: The Restoration of the Davidic Dynasty 9:11a

subject: OT
topic: The Prophet Malachi
front: What does the name Malachi mean, and what is debated about it?
back: "My Messenger". Scholars debate whether it is the prophet's actual name or a title designating his office; those holding it to be a title have suggested Ezra the Scribe. Many scholars believe it was in fact his name.
excerpt: His Name: The name MALACHI means "My Messenger".

subject: OT
topic: The Ministry of Malachi
front: What are the three indications for dating Malachi's ministry?
back: He mentions a "governor" over the land (1:8), a post-exilic condition; he is later than Haggai and Zechariah, who prophesied at the building of the temple, 520-516 B.C.; and details link him to the latter years of Nehemiah's governorship, probably a few years after 433 B.C.
excerpt: First, the Prophet must have prophesied after the exile because he mentions a "governor" as being over the land (1:8).

subject: OT
topic: The Ministry of Malachi
front: When was Nehemiah governor in Jerusalem?
back: He came to Jerusalem as governor in 445 B.C., served some years, and returned temporarily to Persia in 433 B.C. On his return he found gross sin and violation of the Law (Neh. 13).
excerpt:
Nehemiah came to Jerusalem to be governor in 445 Be. He served in that capacity for some 
years and then returned temporarily to Persia in 433 B.C. (Nehemiah 5:14).

subject: OT
topic: The Ministry of Malachi
front: What follows the Book of Malachi?
back: Malachi is the last prophet of the Old Testament and his book ends the Old Testament revelation. There follow four hundred years of silence, after which John the Baptist appeared to prepare the way for the Messiah.
excerpt:
There is then the four hundred years of silence after which the Prophet John the 
Baptist appeared on the scene to "prepare the way" for the Messiah the Lord Jesus Christ.

subject: OT
topic: The nature of His Message
front: What is the nature of Malachi's message?
back: It is exhortative — preaching to the present needs of the people and challenging them to repent and be genuine in their religious and spiritual life — and it also deals with predictive prophecies concerning the Messiah.
excerpt:
the message of Malachi is Exhortative in nature. That is, he preached to the present 
needs of the people and challenged them to repent of their sins, and to be genuine in their 
religious and spiritual life.

subject: OT
topic: The nature of His Message
front: What is the theme of the Book of Malachi, and into what is it developed?
back: "God's Rebuke of Israel's Outrageous Sins", developed into six charges: Israel has doubted God's love, despised God's Name, defied God's Law, disdained God's Justice, disregarded God's Tithes and discredited God's service.
excerpt:
The theme of the Book of Malachi is "God's Rebuke of Israel's Outrageous Sins". 
This theme is developed into six charges against the Nation:

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
front: What does the Hebrew word Massa, "oracle", mean in Malachi?
back: A "burden" imposed by a master, ruler or deity on his subjects: a message laid on the messenger's heart which he is obliged to accept and discharge.
excerpt:
The 
word "Oracle" as used in Malachi means a "burden" imposed by a master or a ruler or a deity 
on his subjects.

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
front: How are the words "I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated" to be understood?
back: As preference, not animosity. God's love for Israel is proved by its very existence as a nation, in contrast to Edom, which by Malachi's day was a nation no more.
excerpt: The terms LOVED and HATED could be explained as preference, not animosity.

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
front: How had the priests despised God's Name?
back: By placing defiled, ritually unclean food upon his altar — offering blind, crippled or diseased animals — when the Law of Moses required that only the best be brought as sacrifices.
excerpt: How have the priests despised God's name? By placing defiled (ritually unclean) food upon His altar.

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
front: In what four ways does Malachi describe divorce?
back: As an act of cruelty (2:14), an act of disloyalty (2:14), an act which frustrates God's design for a godly seed (2:15), and an act which God hates — "I hate divorce" (2:16).
excerpt: It is an act of Cruelty 2:14

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
front: On what ground does Malachi condemn mixed marriages?
back: On religious, not racial, grounds. The men of Israel had married the daughters of a strange god — heathen women who were idolaters — and God had prohibited such marriages because they would lead Israel into idolatry.
excerpt:
This is an issue of 
religion. It is marrying people of other Faith which is being condemned and not because 
of ethnicity.

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
front: What is the Hebrew word for tithe, and what does it mean?
back: Ma'aser, meaning a "tenth".
excerpt: The Hebrew word for Tithe is, ma'aser, and it means a 'Tenth'.

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
front: What must Israel do about the tithes, and what does God promise?
back: They must repent and bring the whole tithe into the storehouse; then God will open the windows of heaven and pour out a blessing on them, and remove the chastisement they were experiencing in their agriculture.
excerpt:
They must repent and "bring the whole tithe 
into the store house," If they are willing to do this, God will open the windows of heaven, 
and pour out a blessing on them.

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
front: What is "the Day of the Lord"?
back: An eschatological term for the consummation of the Kingdom of God, God's triumph over his enemies and the deliverance of his people. It begins with the second coming of Jesus Christ and includes the final judgment.
excerpt: THE DAY OF THE LORD is an eschatological term which refers to the consummation of the Kingdom of God and triumph over his enemies and the deliverance of His people.

subject: OT
topic: Conclusion: (Read Malachi 4:4-6)
front: What are the three views concerning the identification of the promised Elijah?
back: That the promise was fulfilled entirely by John the Baptist; that Elijah will someday come personally and minister again; or that one will come in the spirit and power of Elijah, but not Elijah personally.
excerpt: That this promise of the coming of Elijah was fulfilled entirely by John the Baptist

subject: OT
topic: Summary and Conclusion
front: Why is the Book of Malachi described as a bridge?
back: Because it is seen by many as forming a bridge between the Old Testament and the New Testament.
excerpt: The Book of Malachi is seen by many as forming a bridge between the Old Testament and the New Testament.
